subtype: Approach: copying the previous lead's style without fit [Pitfall]
passage:
Kunal: Tell me about the stand-ups.

Jahnavi: My old boss ran a forty-minute stand-up every morning and a tracker that showed everyone's hours. It worked, for a department of thirty senior people. So when I became lead of six of us, all around twenty-five, I copied it. Long daily stand-ups, a strict tracker, updates due by five. Within a fortnight people stopped joking. Updates got short and careful. Nobody raised problems, because everything was being counted. One afternoon a teammate asked, "Are you checking up on us?" and I heard how quiet the room had become. That system suited my boss's group. It didn't suit this one, and I hadn't asked whether it would.

qa.q: How long were the stand-ups run by Jahnavi's old boss?
qa.a: The old boss ran a forty-minute stand-up every morning.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi feel on hearing the teammate ask whether the team was being checked up on?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt shaken and a little ashamed, suddenly hearing how quiet and watched the room had become.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi try to fit the style to this team, and why?
qa.a: Jahnavi could ask the team what kind of updates help them and shorten the stand-ups, because a routine works better when the people using it helped shape it.

qa.q: How did the team experience the new routine?
qa.a: The team felt policed and cautious, so they stopped joking and raised no problems.

grounding: Illustrates a new lead copying an old boss's daily long stand-ups and strict tracking with a young team that feels policed and goes quiet.

subtype: Approach: copying the previous lead's style without fit [Pitfall]
passage:
I'm Dolma, one of five on Trisha's team at the design studio. We're all around twenty-five, and until April we were just colleagues who ate lunch together.
When Trisha became lead, she brought in her old boss's system. Stand-up every morning for forty minutes, each of us reporting every task. A tracking sheet updated by the hour. Messages at nine at night asking why a column was still yellow.
Her old boss had run a team of twenty senior designers. We were five people who used to share chips.
Within three weeks, lunch got quiet. In stand-ups people said "on track" and nothing else. Nobody mentioned problems any more, because every problem became a question in front of everyone. Farhan started eating at his desk.
By May, Trisha looked puzzled and tired. I heard her say to herself, "It worked so well for Meera ma'am." I don't know if she saw why it didn't work for us.

qa.q: How long were the morning stand-ups under Trisha?
qa.a: They were forty minutes every morning.

qa.q: What might Trisha have been feeling by May?
qa.a: She seemed puzzled and tired, confused that her old boss's method wasn't working for her team.

qa.q: What approach would have fit this team better?
qa.a: Short, informal check-ins and asking the team what support they wanted would suit five peers better than strict tracking built for twenty seniors.

qa.q: How does the new style look to Dolma and the team?
qa.a: Dolma sees the team feeling watched and going quiet, with lunch turning silent and people hiding problems.

grounding: Shows a new lead copying her old boss's long daily stand-ups and strict tracking, leaving her small peer-age team feeling policed and silent.

subtype: Approach: copying the previous lead's style without fit [Pitfall]
passage:
Week one. Mahima took over the marketing team of four and did exactly what her previous manager had done at the bigger agency: a daily forty-five-minute stand-up, a shared tracker with hourly updates, and a rule that every change needed her approval. "It worked brilliantly there," she told her friend Kashish.
Week three. The stand-ups dragged. Her team, all her own age and used to deciding things together, gave one-word updates. Nobody suggested ideas any more. A campaign draft sat unapproved for two days because Mahima was in meetings.
Week five. The client asked why the new campaign was late. Mahima asked the team. There was a long silence, then Aman said, "Honestly? We've stopped trying things. It feels like we're being checked on all the time."
Mahima went home and called Kashish. "I copied a style made for thirty people and used it on four." She sounded tired and a little ashamed.

qa.q: How many people were on Mahima's team?
How did Mahima feel when she called Kashish in week five?
qa.a: She sounded tired and a little ashamed, realising she had copied a style that didn't fit.

qa.q: What else could Mahima try with her small team?
qa.a: She could ask the team how they'd like to work and trust them with small decisions, since they were used to deciding together.

qa.q: How might Aman have felt saying the honest answer?
qa.a: Aman likely felt nervous but relieved to finally say the team felt constantly checked on.

grounding: Shows a new lead copying her previous manager's heavy stand-ups and approvals, which made her small peer team feel policed and go quiet.
